attribution.note: These are Marcus's own words in his own post, not the quoted Noble analysis.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps 'a couple years ago', 'conventional wisdom' and 'by their own lights'. It is a two-part observation about an earlier reputation and the state at publication.

contract.note: Reading 'unassailable' as a widely perceived, hard-to-challenge lead is fair and ordinary. Requiring a broad record for 'conventional wisdom' is reasonable. The 2023–2024 window is an evaluator choice.

evidence.note: Reported Feb 11, 2026: OpenAI Korea head says Code Red has not officially ended. This fits 'by their own lights', sixteen days before the post.
Independent Feb 18, 2026 index puts Gemini 3.1 Pro at the top overall, so Google is at least a close frontier competitor.
2024 article describes OpenAI dominance but also challengers and uncertainty. It does not show a widespread belief that OpenAI was unassailable.
May 2024 TIME piece treats OpenAI, Anthropic and Google as co-leaders and calls keeping the lead a struggle. That cuts against a consensus but is a single article.

reviews.rationale: The present-state parts hold: the Code Red was still officially in place in February (e1) and Google was a close frontier competitor (e2). The earlier 'conventional wisdom that OpenAI was unassailable' is not established from a broad record (e3, e4 show leadership only), and nothing shows it misrepresents views either. Nothing is contradicted, so this is not mixed; the conjunctive claim stays unresolved.

contract.note: Asking for a link from unreliability to willingness to pay to profitability is a fair reading. Calendar 2025 is a reasonable evaluator-chosen period.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own disclosure that hallucinations persist. It shows a reliability limit but says nothing about payment or profit.
Survey of general generative-AI users links hallucination risk to attitudes and continued-use intent. It is not OpenAI-specific and has no payment-ceiling or financial link.

reviews.rationale: The packet shows OpenAI products still make errors and that hallucination concerns weigh on user attitudes in general. Nothing measures OpenAI-specific willingness to pay limited by unreliability, or ties it to 2025 profitability. Nothing contradicts the claim either.

contract.note: Reading 'expensive to operate' as serving costs that materially impede profit is fair. The missing profit basis and the operating-versus-training split mean interpretation matters.

evidence.note: Epoch estimate (published before the cutoff): GPT-5 bundle gross margin about 30%, operating ex-R&D about break-even. This fits the mechanism, but it covers part of 2025 on an estimated basis and partly cuts against 'expensive'.
Anonymous-source report of 2025 revenue of $13.1B and cash burn of $8B. Cash burn does not isolate operating costs or net income.

reviews.rationale: Estimated inference costs take a large share of revenue, and operating margin before R&D is near zero (e3). But this is a partial-year estimate on no matching basis. Positive gross margins also suggest the losses may come mainly from R&D and other costs. There is no reconciled 2025 record that settles the causal contribution.

contract.note: Defining moat, price war and the causal chain this way is fair and ordinary. Separating efficiency-driven cuts from competitive ones is a reasonable requirement.

Preprint finds falling inference prices come from economic forces and efficiency gains. It offers an alternative mechanism but is not specific to OpenAI.

reviews.rationale: Price cuts happened (e5), but nothing ties them to competitive pressure from the lack of a moat rather than efficiency gains (e6). Nothing measures their effect on 2025 profitability. The evidence neither establishes nor refutes the causal chain.
